sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI-generated videos often depict people within detailed scenes while leaving their small facial regions poorly resolved. Visual super-resolution can sharpen these regions without resolving whether the recovered lips and teeth agree with the spoken audio. We present an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that addresses this ambiguity within a reference-guided video flow model. Source--noise mixing initializes reconstruction from a partially preserved observation, and structured reference injection separates appearance anchors from continuous motion context. Training combines restoration of degraded images and videos with correction of degraded dubbed sources under target audio. Appearance and synchronization supervision allow the model to recover facial detail and support visual dubbing when the audio is replaced. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the best paired perceptual similarity and synchronization scores among the compared restoration methods. Component comparisons examine audio conditioning, the reconstruction formulation, and reference injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage. injection. Visual super-resolution can sharpen these regions without resolving whether the recovered lips and teeth agree with the spoken audio. We present an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that addresses this ambiguity within reference-guided video flow model. Sourcenoise mixing initializes reconstruction from partially preserved observation, and structured reference injection separates appearance anchors from continuous motion context. Training combines restoration of degraded images and videos with correction of degraded dubbed sources under target audio. Appearance and synchronization supervision allow the model to recover facial detail and support visual dubbing when the audio is replaced. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the best paired perceptual similarity and synchronization scores among the compared restoration methods. Component comparisons examine audio conditioning, the reconstruction formulation, and reference injection. Native AIGC examples further illustrate the recovery of lip contours, dental structure, and surrounding facial texture in scene-level footage. sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video generation models can synthesize detailed scenes and coordinated character motion [1], yet highresolution frame does not necessarily contain high-resolution face. In medium shots and full-body compositions, faces occupy only small fraction of the image. Lip contours, individual teeth, and the oral cavity can remain blurred or poorly separated even when the surrounding scene is convincing. These defects become prominent during close viewing and reframing. Improving facial quality without regenerating an otherwise satisfactory shot is therefore an important step in downstream AIGC production. Video super-resolution addresses missing visual detail. SeedVR2 [2] uses generative priors for reconstruction, FlashVSR [3] targets efficient streaming restoration, and SparkVSR [4] introduces sparse high-quality keyframes for appearance control. For speaking face, the desired detail also depends on articulation: lip contact determines tooth visibility, while mouth opening changes oral boundaries and occlusion. plausible dental pattern can therefore disagree with the spoken sound. The restoration target must account for audio as well as visual appearance. Audio provides information that can constrain this otherwise ambiguous reconstruction. Extreme-scale talkingface upsampling [5] combines audio with high-resolution identity image; MDVD-Net [6] exploits multimodal cues for compressed face video; and GAVN [7] models temporal and identity information. We focus on low-quality AIGC faces whose observed oral structures or articulation may be unreliable. In this setting, restoring sharp *Corresponding author 1 TaoMate-FVSR Technical Report November Figure 1. Audio-guided facial restoration from AIGC footage. Small facial regions provide limited evidence for lip and teeth structure. The model restores these regions using reference frames and accompanying audio. The three clips illustrate the source scenes and reconstructed heads; the reference bank depicts training-time conditioning. Quantitative references originate from the GT first frame. Cat denotes channel-wise fusion implemented by separate linear projections and summation. version of the source mouth is not always sufficient. The recovered lips and teeth must remain compatible with the accompanying audio throughout the reconstructed sequence. We address this problem with reference-guided video flow model that uses audio during restoration. Its reconstruction trajectory begins from sourcenoise mixture, preserving useful observations without making the source mouth fixed target. Training first pairs degraded images and videos with clean targets. Audio-guided training additionally uses degraded dubbed sources whose mouth configuration differs from the target, requiring the model to follow the supplied speech rather than copy the input lips. Figure 1 illustrates the workflow, and Figure 2 details the learning objectives. Reference guidance presents second challenge: reference frame carries particular pose and mouth configuration that may conflict with the current video. We assign independently encoded references and sequenceencoded history to distinct temporal slots. This structured injection provides persistent appearance anchor while retaining recent motion context. It also avoids treating the reference mouth as frame that the output must reproduce. In the quantitative evaluation, the reference source is the GT first frame; the enhanced-reference setting edits this same image. Visual dubbing tests this articulation-control capability under replacement audio. X-Dub [8] develops mask-free mouth editing, while VideoReTalking [9] combines lip editing with identity-aware enhancement. conventional cascade restores appearance and then changes the mouth through separate model. We evaluate whether our restoration framework retains recovered detail while following new audio, comparing it with super-resolution followed by released dubbing models. This complements the original-audio evaluation of facial restoration. The contributions are threefold: An audio-guided facial video restoration framework that uses target speech to resolve ambiguous oral structure in low-quality footage, supporting both original-audio restoration and replacement-audio dubbing. sourcenoise reconstruction formulation trained with visual-restoration and cross-articulation objectives. The latter uses mismatched source and target mouth configurations to supervise articulation correction. Structured reference injection with separate temporal slots for appearance anchors and continuous history. Component comparisons examine its role alongside audio conditioning and the sourcenoise formulation. TaoMate-FVSR

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Technical Report November 2026 Facial and video restoration. Learned facial priors recover detail from degraded observations. GFP-GAN [10] and GPEN [11] use GAN priors, while CodeFormer [12] uses discrete high-quality representations. BSRGAN [13] and Real-ESRGAN [14] provide synthetic degradations for blind super-resolution. Image restoration methods such as StableSR [15], DiffBIR [16], and SUPIR [17] adapt diffusion priors to balance perceptual quality against fidelity to the observed image. Temporal propagation extends restoration to video: BasicVSR++ [18] uses recurrent propagation, RealBasicVSR [19] pre-cleans inputs, and KEEP [20] uses Kalman-inspired propagation. Generative video restoration and reference control. Upscale-A-Video [21] combines temporal diffusion with flow-guided latent propagation. SeedVR [22] uses window-based video diffusion transformer, and SeedVR2 [2] studies one-step adversarial post-training. FlashVSR [3] targets efficient streaming restoration, while SparkVSR [4] propagates sparse high-quality keyframe guidance through low-resolution videos. We instead couple facial-detail recovery with target-audio control and cross-articulation supervision. Visual dubbing. Wav2Lip [23] uses an expert synchronization objective, DINet [24] deforms reference features, and VideoReTalking [9] combines lip editing with identity-aware enhancement. LatentSync [25] and MuseTalk [26] operate in latent space; X-Dub [8] develops mask-free dubbing through generative bootstrapping. Unlike portrait animation such as AniPortrait [27] and EMO [28], editing an existing video requires articulation changes while preserving source pose and non-articulatory motion. Audio-assisted restoration. Audio can also constrain restoration. Extreme-scale talking-face upsampling [5] combines low-resolution video, audio, and an identity image. MDVD-Net [6] uses audio, geometry, and codec cues; GAVN [7] models complementary temporal and identity information. We focus on restoration when the observed mouth is unreliable or incompatible with replacement audio, and evaluate both original-audio reconstruction and cross-audio dubbing within the same framework.

Source-noise strength 𝜌 [0.80, 0.95] controls retained source evidence; the separate flow time 𝜎 locates point on the target-to-source trajectory. Unlike the image degradation operator, this mixing defines the latent reconstruction trajectory: source structure remains available, while the output need not reproduce unreliable mouth details. Stage 1 jointly trains on degraded images and videos with their corresponding targets. Images use only flow-matching MSE (LMSE) and RGB losses; videos additionally use temporal supervision. Stage 2 uses degraded dubbed sources and target audio for lip correction. Sparse references and continuous history occupy distinct conditioning slots. We therefore inject it as an appearance condition, not prescribed output frame. Sparse clean frames anchor identity and texture, while separate sequence of four adjacent frames supplies local motion context. Each sparse frame is encoded independently, and history is encoded as sequence. Their features occupy disjoint temporal positions in reference canvas; unused positions are zero. shared projection adds this canvas to the DiT input features without replacing the denoising state with reference or history latents. The reference is thus available throughout reconstruction without forcing the output to copy its mouth configuration. Training uses 77-frame windows corresponding to 20 temporal latents. Appearance and history conditions are independently dropped with probabilities 0.1 and 0.4; audio-conditioned training additionally drops audio with probability 0.1. This conditioning dropout discourages dependence on single cue. Reconstruction supervision. For video examples, flow supervision learns the latent reconstruction trajectory while decoded losses constrain appearance and temporal changes: Lrec = Lflow + 0.1LRGB + 0.1LΔ + 0.1LLPIPS. RGB MSE preserves image structure, LPIPS [30] supervises perceptual appearance, and LΔ matches adjacent-frame differences. Still images use only Lflow + 0.1LRGB, without perceptual or temporal losses. The articulationcorrection objective uses dubbed source 𝑋 dub and clean target 𝑌 that share the person and scene but differ in articulation. We degrade the dubbed source to obtain 𝑋 = (𝑋 dub) and condition reconstruction on the audio of 𝑌 . Reproducing the source mouth is therefore insufficient: the target requires both detail recovery and change in oral configuration. With sourcenoise mixing, oral configuration is reconstructed rather than fixed by the input. Frozen HuBERT [31] features pass through trainable audio projection and condition the DiT on the video timeline. The projection aligns speech features with the reconstruction windows, providing an audio condition alongside the visual inputs. Synchronization complements the paired losses: Lstage2 = Lrec + 𝜆syncLsync. (4) We use frozen SyncNet for synchronization supervision, following Wav2Lip [23]. For quantitative evaluation, Ours uses the GT first frame, whereas Ours+ uses its GPT-Image-enhanced version. Both configurations use 512 512 references and the same sampler, without output post-processing. For native AIGC footage without GT, the reference is prepared from the input first frame. Appearance and motion conditioning. For subsequent window 𝑘, let 𝜏 denote the index of the last retained output frame from the preceding window. We combine the fixed appearance reference with the four most recent reconstructed frames to form the next windows conditioning sequence: 𝑃𝑘 = (cid:2)𝑟, ˆ𝑦 𝜏3, ˆ𝑦 𝜏2, ˆ𝑦 𝜏1, ˆ𝑦 𝜏 (cid:3) . (5) The reference is encoded independently to provide appearance guidance, while the second temporal latent of 𝐸 (𝑃𝑘) supplies recent motion context. These features populate their respective conditioning slots. The initial window uses five copies of 𝑟 because no generated history is available. Subsequent windows use only previously reconstructed frames, without future target frames. Boundary conditioning and latent continuation. The last retained RGB frame is also encoded independently as 𝐸 ( ˆ𝑦 𝜏), providing an additional appearance condition at the transition to new content. Although this frame is part of 𝑃𝑘, its independent encoding serves different role from the sequence-encoded motion context. Within the overlapping region, the preceding windows latent trajectory is replayed at matching flow times. Source observations, noise, and audio conditions remain aligned to the same video timeline. Stateful decoding and output assembly. The causal-VAE decoder processes the first window and preserves its internal state when decoding newly retained latents from subsequent windows. Each window contains five conditioning frames and 72 payload frames; stride 56 gives 16 overlapping payload frames. Discarding the conditioning prefix and duplicated overlap yields the original video duration. No RGB cross-fading or histogram matching is applied.

This variant restores the degraded video using visual and reference conditions without audio. In Figure 4, row 2, column 6, its mouth opening is narrower than GT in column 2; Ours in column 4 reconstructs the open-mouth configuration. Although the visual-only variant attains slightly higher PSNR, its Sync-C/D of 4.283/10.524 is worse than 7.621/7.560 for Ours. Its fidelity advantage is limited to 0.26 dB in PSNR and 0.0037 in SSIM, while LPIPS remains nearly unchanged (0.0856 versus 0.0850). The larger synchronization difference, together with the visible mouth-opening error, distinguishes articulation recovery from overall pixel fidelity. Audio supplies complementary information for reconstructing mouth configurations that degraded visual evidence alone leaves ambiguous. Replacing sourcenoise mixing: X-Dub (adapted). We compare our reconstruction formulation with restorationadapted X-Dub [8]. This variant incorporates our reference-frame injection logic: the GT first frame is encoded independently and placed in the appearance-conditioning slot, while motion history occupies separate temporal slot. It receives the same GT first frame and audio as Ours. Instead of sourcenoise mixing, reconstruction starts from Gaussian noise, with the degraded video supplied through dense latent conditions. The appearance reference thus remains explicitly available while the source enters through different conditioning route. This comparison examines an alternative source-conditioning strategy for recovering the target face from degraded observation. Figure 4. Qualitative ablation comparison. Each row shows two selected frames from one clip: MEAD [32] (top) and HDTF [33] (bottom). The same frame pair is displayed for GT and each model variant, with ten images per row. All variants use the GT first frame, and predictions are extracted directly from native RGB outputs. TaoMate-FVSR Technical Report November 2026 Despite higher MUSIQ and CLIP-IQA scores, the adapted model matches the reference appearance less closely. Figure 4, row 1, columns 910, shows over-emphasized skin texture; row 2, column 10, exhibits coarse facial detail and hard dental edges. Its PSNR/LPIPS of 26.63/0.1523, versus 29.10/0.0850 for Ours, reflects greater reconstruction error. Sync-C/D is also worse, at 7.407/8.144. These results favor our sourcenoise formulation over the adapted dubbing formulation for preserving facial appearance while following audio. Stronger apparent sharpness alone does not recover the references skin texture or dental boundaries. Replacing structured reference injection: DirectMotion. DirectMotion replaces the structured reference canvas with direct motion-frame conditioning. The first window repeats the GT first frame five times; subsequent windows use the preceding outputs last five frames. Thus, later windows carry forward generated appearance instead of receiving persistent, independently injected GT first frame. This changes how the model accesses the fixed reference as reconstruction proceeds. In Figure 4, row 1, columns 78, facial texture becomes overly smooth, while row 2, columns 78, exhibits artificial dot patterns. Both are consistent with errors accumulating through generated history and weakening the reference condition. DirectMotion obtains PSNR/LPIPS of 28.24/0.1341, compared with 29.10/0.0850 for Ours. Its Sync-C/D of 7.254/7.875 also trails Ours at 7.621/7.560. The results support structured reference injection: an appearance anchor remains directly accessible in later windows, instead of being inherited only through previously generated frames.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We present facial video restoration framework in which target audio participates directly in reconstruction. The original-audio comparison yields lower paired perceptual error and better synchronization scores than the evaluated restoration baselines. Replacement-audio experiments examine visual dubbing without separate mouth-editing model, and native AIGC examples illustrate recovery of facial regions within larger scenes. Component comparisons connect the observed behavior to audio conditioning, sourcenoise mixing, and structured reference injection. Together, these results support reference-guided approach to downstream facial restoration and dubbing. Reconstructed facial detail is generative estimate, not evidence of true appearance. Because audio-driven editing can facilitate impersonation, applications should obtain appropriate permission and clearly disclose edited content.
